Three men got out and came towards them. The two men from Egulac did not recognize the three men. The three men spoke a strange language that the two men could not understand.

One of the Egulac men picked up a stone and threw it at one of the strangers, and then ran away. The stranger who was hit by the stone fell down. The other two strangers pulled out their bows and arrows and shot the other Egulac man. They left their canoe and went after the first Egulac man. He ran and ran and climbed up a tree. They searched all around the shore for him and then gave up and went back to their canoe and started rowing back to where they came from.
The two Egulac men swam to the place where the three men had landed. They saw that there was a path going through the woods and they followed it. They came to a clearing where there were three teepees. At the far end of the clearing was a large wooden structure that they could not identify. They crept forward to look into the windows of the building and saw three men inside, two on each side of a table and one at the head. One of the Egulac men pointed to the man at the head and whispered to the other, "That's the one. That's how they killed him. He didn't even struggle."

The two Egulac men went back to their village and told the others what had happened. The whole tribe was mobilized in a matter of minutes. They loaded their weapons and prepared to go to war. They traveled all day and all night until they came to the village of the three men. They surrounded the village and waited until the three men came out. Then they attacked.

We will give you a canoe that will carry you and your family and your friends. We will give you a canoe that will carry you to other villages and to the fishing places along the river. We will give you a canoe that will carry you to the sunset and to the morning light." And so they traded canoes. And the men from Kesh were happy and the men from Egulac were happy. And that is how the friendship of two men from different villages began. And that is how the story of the canoe came to be told.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter, and they were forced to swim for their lives to the shore. One of them made it to shore safely, but the other was swept out to sea. The next morning, the survivor went back to where their shelter had been and found that a bird had built a nest in the place where he had been sleeping. The bird was a seagull, and it had three eggs. The man left them alone, and soon the seagull hatched her young.
One day, as he was watching his three seagull children playing along the shore, a thought occurred to him. He wondered if the storm had killed his companion and caused his death. He knew that storms could be deadly, and he might have been killed by the storm while his companion was swept out to sea. But then he thought, "I cannot possibly be the only one this has happened to. There must have been others who have gone through the same experience." And he began to feel better.
But just as he was thinking that he saw something moving in the water. It was his companion, covered with seaweed and struggling to stay afloat. He threw down his belongings and swam out to him. They clung to each other in the water, happy to be together again. From then on, they always took shelter on the shore during storms. And they were never separated again.
The two men from Egulac became the progenitors of a new race of people. They were the first of the Haida, or as they were later called, the "Long-Haired People." They were the ancestors of the Haida, Tlingit, and other Northwest Coast tribes. And so, through their experience of the storm and its aftermath, they came to be.

Then they saw a canoe approaching. It was canoed by Nagosh, the great chief of Egulac. He was very angry when he saw his two young rivals.

Nagosh pulled in his canoe and took out his weapon and shot the third man, Woolak, as he came running out from behind the rock. Then he shot Eylak as he tried to swim away. He did not shoot Egush, however, because he did not want to kill him. He took him back to Egulac and made him a slave.

The two men in the story are symbolic. Eylak represents the lower self, or the ego. Nagosh represents the higher self, or the Superconscious. Woolak represents the unconscious. The story shows the conflict between the lower self and the higher self, and how the higher self must be awakened within the individual. The shooting of Woolak represents the purging of the unconscious, and the enslavement of Egush represents the control of the lower self by the higher self.

They reached the canoe and the men said, "We want to paint your bodies for the initiation ceremony." One of the swimmers said, "I'm not ready for that." The other said, "I'm ready." So the men painted the body of Chontel and not his friend.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylak, friends of the Muskrat people. They were very strong swimmers and could dive deep into the water. They had been out gathering reeds for their houses and had capsized their canoe. They were very good swimmers and could dive deep into the water. They were trying to get to the other side of the river to their village, but the wind had come up and they were having a hard time getting there.
The two men helped the women into their canoe and took them to the other side of the river. They were very happy to be rescued. The men and women were all friends. They went their way and the women went their way.
From that night on, the two men swam less often at night. They were afraid that they might see the women drowning again and that they might not be able to help them.

The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles. The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called to his friend for help, but the older man refused to enter the water, claiming that it was too dark and that there might be other crocodiles in the water. The younger man was unable to swim to the bank because of the strong current and he died as a result of his injuries. 
The older man was criticised by the Egulac tribe for not helping his younger companion, and he replied that he had tried to warn the younger man to avoid the danger. The elder explained that he had been a warrior in his youth and had fought many battles. He had lost his right arm and had been scarred severely on his left arm and leg. He had been made a chief because of his bravery, but he was no longer a young man and had to be careful not to endanger himself and his family. The older man's daughter was married to a man of another tribe, and they had a son who was very young. The older man did not want to risk his own life to attempt to save his son-in-law, who was a coward and would probably run away if attacked. The older man's grandson was very young and would be endangered if they both died. In addition, the older man believed that his younger companion had been careless and had brought his death upon himself. 
In the mythology of the Yukon First Nations peoples, the story of "One Night Two Men" is often told as a cautionary tale about the consequences of being careless or reckless.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter, and they were forced to swim for their lives to the shore. One of them made it to shore safely, but the other was swept out to sea. The next morning, the survivor went back to where they had been sheltering and found that the storm had carried his companion out to sea and he could see him lying on the shore of an island a long way out in the ocean. So he decided to try to swim to him. But midway across the ocean, the storm came up again and knocked him off his course. He struggled through the storm and finally made it to the island, but by the time he got there his companion had been carried out to sea again by the storm and was nowhere to be seen. 

There are many versions of this story. In some tellings, the two men are said to have been friends or lovers. In others, the survivor feels guilty for having left his companion behind and goes back to save him, only to lose him again. And in some versions, the companion who is left behind is said to have been trapped and killed by the storm. 

The story has been retold in many parts of the North Atlantic, including Labrador, Newfoundland, and the Atlantic coast of Canada and the United States. It is also said to be one of the most widely distributed of all Native American stories.

The younger man struggled across the river and was greatly relieved to feel the ground under his feet. He looked up to see his friend standing on the bank, a bow and quiver of arrows in his hand. 
The older man explained that he had seen the shadow of the crocodile as it swam across the moonlit river and had shot it with his bow. They made their way back to the safety of their village, and the younger man was greatly relieved to be alive. From then on, he always swam with a friend, and never again went swimming at night.

The lesson of the story is that it is better to be safe than sorry. The story also shows the importance of experience and knowledge. The older man's caution may have saved the younger man's life.

He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim towards the moon and stars, and I will meet you on the other side." The younger man struggled across the river and was greatly relieved to feel the ground beneath his feet.

The older man replied, "It is better to be safe than sorry."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they knew that the sound was too far away for it to be a war-party, and they were right. It was a peace-party. The two canoes approached each other in the fog, and then they met, and they exchanged gifts, and they smoked the pipe of peace. But one of the parties had brought his woman, and the other party had brought his mother, and the woman of the first party saw the mother of the second party, and the two women began to dance and sing, and the men knew that this was a war-party. And so it was, and the two parties fought all night, and in the morning they parted, and the sun rose, and they saw that it was a full moon night, and they knew that the women had been dancing all night long. And that is how the war-party was discovered, and that is how the two men from Egulac became enemies.

The older man called out to his friend, "Swim towards the moon and stars, and I will meet you on the other side." The younger man struggled across the river and was greatly relieved to feel the ground under his feet. He looked up to see his friend standing on the bank, a bow and quiver full of arrows in his hand.
The older man explained that he had seen the shadow of the crocodile as it swam across the moonlit river and had shot it with his bow. They made their way back to the safety of their village, and the younger man was greatly relieved to be alive. From then on, he always swam with a friend, and never again went swimming at night.

The lesson of the story is that it is better to be safe than sorry. The story also shows the importance of experience and knowledge. The older man's caution may have seemed unnecessary to the younger man, but it ultimately saved his life.

This story is a variation of the one that appears in Mark Twain's 1893 book My Debut as a Literary Person with Other Essays and Stories. Twain credits the story to a friend and mentor, George B. Cudjoe, who told it to him during a trip down the Mississippi River.

The older man explained that he had seen a group of crocodiles on the opposite bank, and that he intended to shoot them while they were still weakened by the light of the moon. He pointed out that the crocodiles would be able to see the younger man as clearly as he could see them, and that they would be coming to attack him.
The younger man realized that his friend had saved his life by warning him of the danger and then guiding him to safety. He was filled with awe and gratitude for his friend's intelligence and quick thinking. From then on, the two men worked together closely, hunting and fishing and protecting each other from danger.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylak. They were very strong swimmers and they raced each other across the river. One morning, as they got up from their wrestling, they saw a canoe coming across the river. They greeted the occupants and found out that it was Canon and his son Kiva. Canon was the ruler of all the villages around the river and he was very powerful. He asked them why they were wrestling all night long. They told him that they were just having a contest to see who was stronger. Canon was very angry and he said, "From this moment on, you will be like two brothers. You will share everything you have with each other. You will share your food, your women, and your children. You will be like two hands on one body." From that day on, the two men were like two hands on one body. They did everything together and nothing could come between them. They were true friends until the day they died.

They were able to escape to the safety of their village, but they were wet and cold and exhausted. One of the men, Dagool, was sick and could hardly move. His companion, Gootah, tried to dry his clothes and warm him up, but after a while he saw that Dagool was dead. He felt very alone and lost. Then he heard a voice calling to him. It was the voice of his wife, calling from the safety of their village. She told him that she had seen the storm coming and had tried to find him to warn him, but she could not find him. She told him that the storm was sent by the gods to punish him for hunting seals, and that he must come home now and never hunt seals again. Gootah started toward the village, but as he was crossing the river a second storm came up. He was washed downstream, and when he finally reached the village he found that it was under attack by a group of warriors from a neighboring village. He fought his way through them and finally reached the safety of his own village, where he was welcomed home by his wife.

His friend replied, "I did not know it was your time to die."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves on an island in the river, and in the morning they found that a canoe had appeared beside their shelter. They decided to take the canoe and the contents back to their village, but when they got there they found that the Egulac people were at war with a neighboring tribe and that the tribal law said that anyone bringing a canoe back to the village would be killed. So they lived on the matches until the war was over.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.

The lesson of this story is that experience and knowledge are valuable and can save lives. The younger man in the story had been cocky and laughed at his friend's caution. He learned from experience that his friend's knowledge and experience were valuable and that he had much to learn.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim towards the moon and stars, and I will meet you on the other side." The younger man struggled across the river and was greatly relieved to feel the ground beneath his feet. 
As he and his friend walked away from the river, the younger man said, "I was wrong to laugh at your caution. From now on I will always watch the position of the moon and stars." 
The older man replied, "It is better to be safe than sorry."

Source:
An African folktale, retold by Joseph Jacobs, "One Night Two Men," in The Golden Age of Folk-Lore, vol. 5, London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1909, pp. 267-269.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter, and they were forced to swim for their lives to the shore. One of them made it to shore safely, but the other was swept out to sea. The next morning, the survivor went back to where they had been sheltering and found that the storm had deposited a large number of seals on the beach. He collected as many of them as he could, and then went back to Egulac. When he told what had happened, they went out to the beach where they saw that a large number of seals had been stranded there. They collected as many of them as they could, and then went home. The following day, the same two men went down to the beach to look for seals, but the water was rough and they could not find any. They decided to go out to the edge of the ice and hunt for seals there. They had hardly gone out half a mile when the ice broke and they were forced to swim for their lives. They climbed onto an island near where they had been hunting, and as they were looking for a place to shelter, the storm came up again. They spent the night on the island, and in the morning they found that the storm had washed away the bridge that connected the island to the mainland. They spent the day waiting for the bridge to be washed back into place, and in the evening they heard the sound of people talking. They went to the place where the bridge had been and found that the people of Egulac had come to look for them. They were taken back to the mainland, and from then on they never went out to hunt seals in the winter.

The older man was criticised by the Egulac tribe for not helping his friend when he was in danger. However, the older man argued that he had done all he could to save his friend. He had warned him of the danger and had tried to convince him not to swim across the river. He argued that his friend had made him promise not to enter the water unless it was daylight, and that he (the older man) had kept his promise. The tribe elders decided that the older man was correct and that the younger man had been responsible for his own death. 
This story is similar to the tale of the Two Brothers from the Māori people of New Zealand. In this story a younger brother goes out hunting and is attacked and eaten by a taniwha, a large mythical serpent. The older brother seeks revenge and tricks the taniwha onto a sandbar, where he cuts off its head. The marrow inside the taniwha's spine is considered the cause of death, as the taniwha's spirit lives within the marrow. The older brother then takes the taniwha's teeth and nails and uses them to create the North Island and the South Island of New Zealand.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". But they looked, and saw that there were only two canoes, and they were pulled by women. And they thought: "Maybe this is a dream". Then one of them stood up and was shot, and the other one returned home. And he told what had happened: "While we were hunting seals, the sun went down, and we were adrift in the fog, and we heard war-cries, and saw two canoes pulling women, and the man in one of the canoes shot me." He told it all, and then he died.

Discussion:
This story is a classic example of a "two men" story, a type of narrative that has two protagonists who go on a journey and usually end up dead. In this case, the two men are hunting seals when they encounter a war party of women. One of the men is killed, and the other returns home to relate the story to his tribe. The source notes that this story is a "version" of the one told by Chief Sitting Bull, although it is substantially different. This version has the men killed by women, which is unusual for the genre, and the survivors return home to relate the story to their tribe. Most "two men" stories have the men killed by other men, and the survivors usually die as well, often with their bodies found by their tribes. The reason for the killing in this story may be the men's hunting of seals

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter and almost killed them. They were able to escape to the safety of their village, but they were wet and cold and exhausted. One of the men, Dagool, was sick and could hardly move. His companion, Ganada, had to carry him on his back all the way to their village. When they arrived, the woman of the village took one look at Dagool and knew that he was sick with smallpox. She took him inside and looked after him, and soon he was well again.
The two men of Egulac were very grateful to the woman for saving Dagool's life, and they stayed with her for three days and three nights, hunting seals for her. And then they left, going back to their own village. From then on, every year when the men of Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals, they would stop at the village of the woman who had saved Dagool's life, and they would give her one half of all the seals they had caught. And that is why, when the white men came to Egulac and asked the people where they came from, they said: "From the village of the smallpox woman."

Notes
"One Night Two Men from Egulac" is a traditional story of the Muskrat people. The story is over 1,000 words long and is printed in the book First Nations Stories by James Wood. The story is printed in English and in Syilx (Okanagan). The Syilx version of the story is printed using the Syilx Orthography.

Then they stood up and they faced the river and they raised their hands. And the water came up to them and it carried them away.

Ganada told Dagool that he believed the dream meant that they would soon find a place where they could live without having to hunt seals anymore. The story, "One Night Two Men from Egulac," is a short story written by Frank R. Stockton. It was first published in The National Police Gazette on November 23, 1907, and was later collected in his 1911 book The Best Stories of Frank R. Stockton. It is one of the more frequently anthologized of Stockton's works. The story is a example of the type known as a "buddy story," and has been adapted for film several times. The most notable version was directed by John Ford in 1936, with Henry Fonda and George O'Brien.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eyash, young and strong swimmers, who made their living transporting passengers and cargo in their canoes. As they swam in the dark, suddenly a monster came up behind them and grabbed Egush by the leg. Egush struggled and fought with all his might, but the monster was too strong. Eyash saw this and swam up to the monster, pulling out his knife, he stabbed the monster in the heart, killing it. The monster fell apart, and in the morning they found that it was a giant eel.

The two men were very frightened, and they decided to go to the village and warn the other people about the eel. As they were pulling their canoe onto the shore, the eel came up again, blocking their way. Eyash took his knife and stabbed the eel's heart, killing it. The eel fell apart, and the two men ran to the village to warn the others.

When they arrived, the villagers did not believe them. They said that there was no way that a giant eel could exist. The two men knew that they would have to prove the villagers wrong. So they went down to the river, and sure enough, there was another giant eel waiting for them. Eyash killed it with his knife, and this time the villagers came out to see what had happened. When they saw the dead eel, they were shocked and amazed, and they finally believed the two men.

From then on, the two men were known as the heroes of the village. They had saved the people from the giant eels, proving their strength and bravery. From that day on, no one doubted that they were the strongest swimmers in all the land.

The village was quiet as everyone prepared to leave this world. The men built a large bonfire and everyone gathered around it. They sang songs and they danced. They swam to the canoe and they pushed their sisters away. They swam back to the bank and they ran into the woods. Their sisters called to them from the canoe. They begged them to come back. They said they would be killed if they did not come back. The men were afraid. They hid. Their sisters searched for them. They looked for them along the river. They looked for them in the woods. They called and they called. Finally they gave up their search. The men did not come back. Their sisters went home. The men were safe. But they were not happy. They were afraid their sisters would come back and kill them. They were afraid of their sisters.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim towards the moon and stars, and I will meet you on the other side." The younger man struggled across the river and reached the bank. His friend helped him up and they walked away from the river, leaving the crocodile behind.
In Egulac they talk about this story as a warning to young people to be careful and not to swim in the river at night.

The story, as told here, is a variation of the cautionary tale "The Two Brothers". The tale has been interpreted as a warning against heedless youth and the dangers of the unknown. It has also been used to argue for the importance of experience and knowledge over youthful arrogance.The two brothers are often interpreted to be Adam and Eve, or Adam and Abel, and the crocodile is sometimes seen as a metaphor for a dangerous sexual partner or pregnancy.

Source
Mindlin, Betty. "One Night Two Men." In Stories from the Rivers of Amazon and Congo, edited by Charles L. Porter and Mary C. Porter. Two Worlds, 1987. pp. 173–176. ISBN 978-0912723325.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too late; the moon was now full and the water monsters were out. The younger man scoffed at his friend's superstition and dived into the water. 
While he was underwater a monster grabbed him and dragged him downstream. The older man watched in shock as his friend was taken under. He called out to the spirit of the water, begging for his friend's life.
The spirit of the water released the younger man, but told the older man that he would have to pay a price for his intervention. The younger man was covered in mud and couldn't see where he was going. He stumbled around in the darkness, lost and disoriented.
The older man decided to take his friend home and care for him. It took them three days to travel the river and two months to recover. The younger man never forgot the lesson learned that night: respect the spirits of the land, water, and air.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim to the shore, my young friend. Swim to the shore and live."
The younger man struggled to the shore and was helped out of the water by his friend. As they were walking away from the river, the younger man said, "I was wrong. You were right. I should have listened to you."
"Yes, my friend. That is how it should be."
They walked on in the darkness until they came to a clearing where a village was situated. The younger man said to his friend, "We are lost. We should turn back."
"No, my friend. We are not lost. We are where we are supposed to be."
They continued on through the village until they came to a house where a festival was taking place. The younger man said to his friend, "We have come to the wrong place. We should turn back."
"No, my friend. We are not lost. We are where we are supposed to be."
The older man knew that his friend was blind. He had been leading him to the village so that his friend could enjoy the festival.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim to the shore, my young friend. Swim to the shore and live."
The younger man struggled to the shore and was helped out of the water by his friend. As they were walking away from the river, the younger man said, "Your caution saved my life. I was foolish to laugh at you."
The older man thought for a moment and then said, "It was your laughter that saved my life. For every time I have laughed at your caution, the Great Spirit has sent a thunderbolt to earth."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter and almost killed them. They were able to escape to the safety of their village, but they were so exhausted and weak from fighting the storm that they fell asleep immediately upon entering their village. While they were sleeping, the villagers noticed that there was a glow in the sky, like the glow of a fire. They went to investigate and found the two men lying there weak and exhausted. They helped the men back to their village and fed them. The two men were very grateful and gave thanks to the villagers, saying that they had been saved by the villagers' kindness. From then on, the two men became like brothers to the villagers and lived with them.

This story is one of several that make up the mythology of the Yukon First Nations people. The exact meaning behind the story is unknown, but it is often seen as representing the relationship between the humans and the natural world; how humans must work with nature, and cannot fight against it. The story also represents the idea of community and how important it is for humans to work together.

Source:
Wilson, D. (2010). First Nations Myths and Legends.  Vancouver: Orca Book Publishers.

Alternate versions:
There are many variations of this story. In one version, the two men are hunting for themselves and for their village. In another version, the two men are on a vision quest. In another version still, the two men are brothers. And in a final version, the two men are enemies who become friends through their shared experience. Regardless of the specifics, all versions of the story emphasize the importance of community and working together.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylak, friends since childhood. They swam and they laughed and they sang. They were young and strong and happy. Then they saw a canoe approaching. It was canoed by Nagosh, the great chief of Egulac. He was very angry when he saw his two young rivals.

They went out to the canoe and talked to Nagosh. They listened carefully to what he said. Nagosh was their chief, and they obeyed his orders. But they were very unhappy. They did not think that Nagosh was right. They thought that he was wrong. They wished that they could go back to the way things had been before. But they knew that they could never do that.

The story also shows that although the men lost their bachelorhood, they gained something in return - the story ends on a positive note, implying that the men were happy in their marriages and as fathers.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylak, friends of the Muskrat people. They were very strong swimmers and could dive deep into the water. They had gone down to the river to play and to catch their food. They were naked, and they painted their bodies with clay to protect themselves from the cold. They were very sure of themselves, and they laughed at the Sturgeon and the Pike, the Bear and the Beaver, even at the mighty Eagle, the king of the birds. But the gods heard their laughter and took offence at their presumption. The thunder came, and the lightning, and a great wind blew over the water. The two men were frightened and tried to reach the shore, but the god of the river had taken away their strength. They called to the gods for mercy, and the storm ceased. But the two men were angry with the gods and cursed them, and the gods were angry with the men and cursed them in turn. From that day the Muskrat people have been sick and weak, and they die easily. And from that day, the Sturgeon and the Pike, the Bear and the Beaver, even the Eagle, have grown stronger, and no Muskrat can catch them. And that is the story of the two men from Egulac.

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there a great storm came up. They built a shelter for themselves, but the storm was so violent that it knocked down the shelter, and they were forced to swim for their lives to the shore. One of them made it to shore safely, but the other was swept out to sea. The next morning, they started to look for the missing man. They searched the beach, but they did not find him. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles.
The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. He called out to his friend for help, but his friend had been watching the position of the moon and stars and knew that they had been swimming in the direction of the crocodile's nest. 
The older man called out to his friend, "Swim towards the moon and stars, and I will meet you on the other side." The younger man struggled across the river and reached the bank. His friend helped him up and they walked away from the river, leaving the crocodile behind.
In Egulac they talk about this incident as an example of how important it is to pay attention to the larger context, even when making seemingly small decisions.

And that is why, when the white men came to Egulac and asked the people where they came from, they said: "From the village of the smallpox woman."

One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too dark to see where they were going and that they might be attacked by crocodiles. The younger man laughed at his caution and dived into the river. As he was swimming across the river he was attacked and bitten by a crocodile. The older man was considered a coward by the other villagers, and he was forced to leave Egulac and live in the forest on the outskirts of the village.
One day, many years later, a canoe containing a woman and her baby capsized in the river. The older man was passing by in his canoe and was able to save them both. The woman and her husband were very grateful and offered the older man a place to stay in their village. The older man was overjoyed to be reunited with his old friend's family, and he lived with them for the rest of his life.

Wherever it is told, it is virtually word-for-word the same story. That is quite remarkable for a story that has no moral, no message, and no punch line.

The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too late; the full moon was up and the water monsters were out. The younger man scoffed at this and swam out to the middle of the river where he saw a pair of glowing eyes. He swam back to the bank and told the older man that he had been wrong and that there were no water monsters. Just then a wave came along and washed the younger man back out to the middle of the river, where he was carried downstream by the current. The older man saw this and swam out to his friend. He tried to pull him to safety, but the current was too strong. They struggled for a while, and the older man finally managed to drag his friend to the bank. Exhausted, he lay down on the shore and panted. His friend turned to him and said, "I thought you said there were no water monsters?" The older man replied, "There aren't. Only in stories."

An analysis:
The story seems to be a variation of the cautionary tale "There Are No Water Monsters". The twist in this version is that the older man, far from being proved wrong by the events of the story, is actually the wiser party. Although he believes in the existence of water monsters, he knows that they are not a threat to swimmers, and his friend learns this lesson the hard way. The story may also be a commentary on the dangers of mockery; the younger man's scoffing at his friend's warning is what gets him killed.

The younger man was preparing to dive into the water when the older man warned him that it was too late; the moon was now full and the water monsters were out. The younger man scoffed at his friend's superstition and dived into the river. 
While he was underwater a monster grabbed him and dragged him away. The older man jumped into the river and tried to follow his friend, but the monster was too fast for him. He called out to the spirits for help.
The spirits sent a flock of birds to the surface. The younger man was trapped in the monster's house at the bottom of the river. The older man threw sticks and stones at the monster's house, and the spirits of the birds hit the house from the other side. The monster was angry and came out of his house, but the spirits of the birds hit him so hard on the head that he let go of the younger man.
The younger man swam to the surface, exhausted and scared. The older man helped him out of the water and they went back to their village. The younger man was still shaking from fear and the older man asked him what it was that he was so afraid of. The younger man told him that he was afraid of the monster in the river.
The older man told him that there are two kinds of monsters in the world: those who kill people and those who help people. The monster in the river is the kind that helps people. He saves people from drowning, but he only does this every full moon. The younger man realized that he had almost been saved by the monster. From then on he didn't scoff at his friend's superstitions anymore.
